Roadmap Upload your own knowledge base — let visitors paste or upload their own documents and run CAG vs RAG on their own content. This turns the app from a fixed demo into a general-purpose evaluation tool, and makes the context-window constraint tangible for any domain. Streaming responses — stream tokens to the UI as they arrive instead of waiting for the full response. CAG's latency disadvantage (30% slower in the sample tournament) is largely a perception problem at full-document scale; streaming would make it feel much faster. Advanced RAG techniques — add re-ranking (Cohere Rerank or a cross-encoder), HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings), or multi-query retrieval to close the accuracy gap. The current RAG pipeline is intentionally simple to make the comparison fair to CAG; a "RAG Pro" mode would show how far retrieval quality can be pushed. Controlled retrieval evaluation — the current setup lets RAG supplement thin retrieved chunks with the model's training knowledge (no explicit "ONLY" restriction), which can inflate RAG scores independent of retrieval quality. Multi-Agent Research Desk Confer Inc. · AI/ML Engineering Take-Home · Assignment 5 of 5 A production-grade pipeline of three cooperating AI agents that research any topic, draft a structured brief, and review it for quality — escalating low-confidence work to a human instead of auto-publishing. Every job flows through a shared Postgres queue; a live board shows each stage in real time. Live board: GitHub: Table of contents 1. What it does 2. Architecture 3. Pipeline flow 4. chunks.title: Take Home Project
chunks.text: Submit a research topic (e.g. "Anthropic Claude vs GPT-4o enterprise adoption 2025") and watch three AI agents cooperate to produce a published brief: 1. Collector — searches the web via Tavily, deduplicates by domain, asks an LLM to score relevance, and selects the 7 best sources. Works for any topic — news, academic papers, technical research. 2. Writer — reads the curated sources and drafts a 900–1,100-word Markdown brief with Summary, Key Findings, and Analysis sections. 3. Reviewer — evaluates the brief against the sources on three checks (citation support, coverage, factuality) and emits a calibrated confidence score. Briefs above 70% confidence auto-publish; below 70% → escalated to a human. Human reviewers can Approve (publish), Reject (fail), or Revise with AI — typing specific instructions that are injected directly into the Writer's LLM prompt for a targeted re-draft. If the revision passes the 70% bar it auto-publishes; if not, it escalates again for another round. Architecture Key design decisions Decision — Rationale.

Google Cloud VPS over Oracle Always-Free — Oracle Always-Free ARM instances had no available capacity in west-coast regions. Google Cloud provided a reliable instance immediately with $300 free credits. See Challenges. Deterministic DB state machine instead of Temporal — Postgres + optimistic locking is durable, crash-safe, and free-tier-friendly. On crash/reboot the orchestrator resumes from the locked stage — no workflow engine needed. Groq API (free tier) — 14,400 tokens/minute, 500K/day. Much faster than Ollama Cloud for the demo window. Supabase realtime — Board updates live without polling — every status change the board receives instantly via websocket. Anon key in browser, service-role on VPS — RLS policies restrict what the browser can do (read-only + submit jobs + insert reviews). The orchestrator bypasses RLS to advance job state. OpenClaw per agent — Each agent has its own workspace with a SOUL.md persona and isolated skills/run.mjs — genuine separation of concerns, not one mega-prompt. Model selection: right-sizing per agent Each agent has different quality requirements and tolerance for latency. We observed a clear ceiling with a uniform small-model approach and made a deliberate change: Observation: Early versions of the pipeline used llama-3.1-8b-instant (8B parameters) for all three agents. The Collector and Reviewer worked well — their tasks are structural (scoring a list, evaluating JSON checks), and the fast model handled them reliably. The Writer, however, consistently produced shallow Key Findings — one-liner bullets despite explicit prompt instructions to write 2–3 sentences per point with context and analysis. The small model would acknowledge the instruction but not follow it: it summarises rather than analyses. Decision: Switch the Writer stage to llama-3.3-70b-versatile (70B parameters, also on Groq free tier) while keeping the Collector and Reviewer on llama-3.1-8b-instant.

chunks.title: Take Home Project
chunks.text: the Writer stage to llama-3.3-70b-versatile (70B parameters, also on Groq free tier) while keeping the Collector and Reviewer on llama-3.1-8b-instant. Reasoning: The Writer is the only quality-critical stage. The brief is the deliverable — graders read it. Shallow Key Findings undermine the entire pipeline's value regardless of how well the other stages perform. The Collector's job is ranking and selection (structural, not generative) — a fast small model is appropriate. The Reviewer's job is JSON evaluation output — it needs to follow a schema, not write prose. A small model is fine. The latency tradeoff is acceptable: the write stage increases from 10s to 45s. The total pipeline goes from 90s to 2 minutes — reasonable for a research brief. Both models sit on the same Groq API endpoint, so no new provider, key, or infrastructure is needed. One env var (WRITERMODEL) selects the model per-agent. Result: The 70B Writer produces detailed, analytical Key Findings — each bullet is a substantive paragraph, not a headline. The Collector and Reviewer remain fast and accurate.

PM2 over systemd The original ops plan used systemd units. In practice, PM2 was simpler for a Node.js process running from a user home directory: built-in log rotation, --update-env to pick up .env changes on restart, and reboot persistence via two commands (pm2 startup + pm2 save) rather than writing a unit file, placing it in /etc/systemd/system/, and managing systemctl enable. The systemd unit remains in infra/ as an alternative. Lesson: systemd is the right tool for system services owned by root; PM2 is the right tool for Node.js application processes owned by a non-root user. Redeploy from scratch

chunks.title: AutoGrader Agent
chunks.text: AutoGrader Agent. AI agent that auto-grades any Jupyter notebook (ML, RAG, NLP, CV, data analysis, algorithms). chunks.text: Super Resolution Using HAN. Super Resolution using HAN (Holistic Attention Network) architecture Super Resolution using Holistic Attention Network (HAN) Deep Learning Project Developed by: Juvenal F Barajas Shivani Bokka Divya Panchal 📌 Introduction Super-resolution (SR) is the process of reconstructing high-resolution (HR) images from low-resolution (LR) inputs. It restores fine details, sharpens edges, and produces clearer visuals. With the rise of deep learning, SR has seen dramatic improvements in quality and scalability. SR is especially important in domains such as: Medical imaging → Enhancing MRI/CT scans for improved diagnostics. Satellite imaging → Improving clarity for terrain/weather/urban studies. Digital photography → Upscaling images without losing detail. Traditional methods (e.g., bicubic interpolation) fall short, while CNN-based methods (e.g., SRCNN) improved performance but lacked depth. More advanced models like HuSusu and RealFormer improved efficiency but couldn’t fully leverage hierarchical feature relationships. Our project implements and evaluates the Holistic Attention Network (HAN) for super-resolution, with modifications to enhance its performance.

chunks.title: Super Resolution Using HAN
chunks.text: nships. Our project implements and evaluates the Holistic Attention Network (HAN) for super-resolution, with modifications to enhance its performance. 🧠 Why HAN? The HAN architecture introduces hierarchical attention mechanisms that capture both global and local features simultaneously. SRCNN → Simple but limited in feature extraction. HuSusu & RealFormer → Stronger, but less effective at capturing hierarchical dependencies. HAN → Uses attention at multiple levels (layer, channel, spatial), leading to sharper, more precise reconstructions. 🔧 Custom modifications in our implementation: Added an extra convolutional layer for deeper feature extraction. Incorporated a batch normalization layer for stability and improved generalization. 📊 Dataset (DIV2K) We trained on the DIV2K dataset, a gold standard in super-resolution research. 1,000 HR images (2000 px resolution). 800 images used for training, 100 images for validation. Data preparation: Generated 500,000 patches (64×64) for localized learning. Applied rotations, flips for augmentation. Normalized pixel values to [0,1] using Min-Max scaling. Downscaled LR images via bicubic interpolation.

chunks.title: Super Resolution Using HAN
chunks.text: ng. Applied rotations, flips for augmentation. Normalized pixel values to [0,1] using Min-Max scaling. Downscaled LR images via bicubic interpolation. ✅ Advantages: diverse content, high fidelity, scalable for multiple SR factors (×2, ×4, ×8). 🏗️ HAN Model Architecture The HAN integrates multiple attention mechanisms: Layer Attention Module (LAM): Selects outputs from the most relevant layers. Channel Attention Module (CAM): Highlights important feature channels (textures, edges). Spatial Attention Module (SAM): Focuses on key spatial regions (edges, contours). Residual Attention (RA): Learns the difference (residual) between LR and HR, improving detail reconstruction. ➡️ Together, they form a hierarchical attention mechanism enabling robust HR reconstruction. 🧪 Training & Experiments We experimented with different hyperparameter setups: Time — Batch Size — numcsams — tmax — Notes. 31 hrs — 150 — 12 — 200 — Moderate convergence. 28.5 hrs — 250 — 5 — 50 — Rapid loss drop, plateau early. 34 hrs — 250 — 5 — 50 — Similar plateau. 68.5 hrs — 25 — 12 — 300 — Smooth, stable. 157 hrs — 45 — 12 — 300 — Stable, but slow. 73.5 hrs — 15 — 15 — 280 — ✅ Best performing configuration.

Best configuration: Batch size = 15 numcsams = 15 tmax = 280 Training time = 73.5 hrs 📈 Results Evaluation Metrics: SSIM (Structural Similarity Index): 0.5607 → Moderate structural similarity. PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio): 20.44 dB → Reasonable pixel fidelity. Benchmark Comparisons (Urban100, Manga109): Bicubic interpolation: lowest scores. SRCNN: Improved, but limited detail. RCAN, D-DBPN: Strong results with advanced architectures. HAN+ (enhanced): Achieved highest PSNR & SSIM among state-of-the-art. Our HAN implementation: Competitive, but below SOTA, due to training resource limits. 🚀 Future Directions To enhance HAN further: Model refinements: explore dual/adaptive attention, deeper residual learning. Generative AI: integrate diffusion models for sharper, more realistic images. Training improvements: longer training on higher-resolution datasets, multi-scale supervision. New applications: extend to outpainting (content generation beyond boundaries). Optimization: compression for real-time deployment on mobile/IoT devices.
